strategy_title: Halve Block Size to Cut Shared Memory Bank Conflicts
strategy_description: When NCU reports severe shared memory bank conflicts (e.g. 17-way conflicts accounting for >80% of shared load wavefronts) and MIO stall cycles dominate CPI, reducing the block size (threads per block) proportionally reduces the number of shared memory requests per block, cutting total bank conflict wavefronts by ~4x and MIO stall cycles from 9.4 to 5.4. The key causal chain is: smaller block → fewer concurrent shared memory accesses per block → fewer conflicting bank accesses → lower MIO stall cycles → lower elapsed cycles. In this case, halving block size from 128 to 64 and doubling BLOCK_K from 32 to 64 (to maintain work per thread) reduced executed instructions by 5.4x and duration by 2.3x, despite the bank conflict ratio remaining at 17-way (the absolute count dropped from 1.16M to 290K).
slow_pseudocode:
# BLOCK_M=16, BLOCK_K=32, block_size=128
@triton.jit
def kernel(...):
    BLOCK_M: tl.constexpr = 16
    BLOCK_K: tl.constexpr = 32
    # 128 threads, 12.29 KB dynamic smem/block
    # 17-way bank conflicts on 82944 shared loads
    for k_idx in range(0, tl.cdiv(K, BLOCK_K)):  # 54 iterations
        a = tl.load(A + ...)
        b = tl.load(B + ...)
        acc += tl.dot(a, b)
applicable_when: NCU reports SharedMemoryConflicts with high bank conflict way (>=8x) and bank conflicts representing >70% of shared load wavefronts; CPIStall rule shows MIO stall cycles are the dominant stall type (>50% of total CPI); L1/TEX Cache Throughput is very high (>80%) indicating shared memory pressure; the kernel has small M dimension (M << BLOCK_M) making BLOCK_M reduction safe.
do_not_apply_when: Kernel is already occupancy-limited and reducing block size would further drop achieved occupancy below a critical threshold; the shared memory bank conflicts are caused by access pattern (stride), not block size — in that case padding shared memory arrays is the correct fix; BLOCK_M reduction would cause significant work imbalance or mask inefficiency (many masked-off threads).
framework_notes: In Triton, BLOCK_M and BLOCK_K are tl.constexpr values set at kernel definition time. Reducing BLOCK_M from 16 to 2 (matching actual M=2) eliminates padding waste and reduces smem footprint. Pairing with @triton.autotune over num_warps and num_stages allows the compiler to find the best configuration for the reduced block size. The tl.max_contiguous/tl.multiple_of hints for memory access were also removed when BLOCK_M was reduced to match M exactly, simplifying the load logic.

strategy_title: Double BLOCK_K to halve K-loop iterations in small matmuls
strategy_description: Doubling BLOCK_K (e.g., 32→64) halves the number of K-loop iterations, reducing loop overhead and total executed instructions (~8.3% fewer instructions observed). This is most beneficial when K is large relative to M and N, and when the kernel is latency-bound rather than throughput-bound. However, enabling TF32 (ALLOW_TF32=True) alongside BLOCK_K doubling did not raise Compute SOL as expected—the kernel remained at ~0.73-0.77% Compute SOL—suggesting the workload is too small (12 blocks, 0.01 waves/SM) for Tensor Core throughput gains to materialize; the modest 4.3% speedup came primarily from reduced instruction count.
slow_pseudocode:
BLOCK_K: tl.constexpr = 32
ALLOW_TF32: tl.constexpr = False
# K-loop runs ceil(K/32) = 54 iterations
for k in range(0, K, BLOCK_K):
    a = tl.load(A_ptr + k_offsets)  # shape [BLOCK_M, BLOCK_K]
    b = tl.load(B_ptr + k_offsets)  # shape [BLOCK_K, BLOCK_N]
    acc += tl.dot(a, b, allow_tf32=ALLOW_TF32)
fast_pseudocode:
BLOCK_K: tl.constexpr = 64
ALLOW_TF32: tl.constexpr = False  # TF32=True had no measurable Compute SOL effect
# K-loop runs ceil(K/64) = 27 iterations
for k in range(0, K, BLOCK_K):
    a = tl.load(A_ptr + k_offsets)  # shape [BLOCK_M, BLOCK_K]
    b = tl.load(B_ptr + k_offsets)  # shape [BLOCK_K, BLOCK_N]
    acc += tl.dot(a, b, allow_tf32=ALLOW_TF32)
applicable_when: Triton matmul kernel with large K relative to M/N; kernel is latency-bound (low waves/SM, low Compute SOL <5%); BLOCK_K can be doubled while still evenly dividing K; shared memory budget allows 2x BLOCK_K tile; instruction count reduction is the primary lever
do_not_apply_when: Kernel is already throughput-bound (Compute SOL >50%); doubling BLOCK_K would exceed shared memory limits and reduce occupancy; K is not evenly divisible by the new BLOCK_K; M or N tiles are already large enough that K-loop overhead is negligible; enabling TF32 is the primary goal (it showed no Compute SOL improvement here at this problem size)
framework_notes: Triton: BLOCK_K is a tl.constexpr; doubling it automatically doubles tl.arange(0, BLOCK_K) offsets. ALLOW_TF32 is passed to tl.dot(allow_tf32=ALLOW_TF32). On H200 with a 12-block grid (0.01 waves/SM), TF32 Tensor Core throughput gains are not observable—the bottleneck is launch/wave underutilization, not instruction throughput.

strategy_title: Doubling BLOCK_N Worsens Smem Conflicts and Register Pressure
strategy_description: Doubling BLOCK_N from 32 to 64 in a tiny Triton matmul (BLOCK_M=2, BLOCK_K=64) increased dynamic shared memory per block from 8.7 KB to 16.9 KB, which raised the bank conflict way from 12 to 17 and increased bank-conflicting wavefronts from 77.78% to 82.35% of all shared loads. Simultaneously, registers per thread nearly doubled from 72 to 126, reducing theoretical occupancy from 37.5% to 20.31% and increasing total executed instructions by ~80%. The net effect was a 26% longer kernel duration despite a modest improvement in Warp Cycles Per Issued Instruction (10.12 → 7.09), because the larger tile created more total work and more severe memory pressure rather than reducing it.
slow_pseudocode:
# BLOCK_N=32, BLOCK_K=64, BLOCK_M=2, block_size=32
# 8.7 KB dynamic smem/block, 72 regs/thread
# 12-way bank conflicts, 77.78% of wavefronts conflicting
BLOCK_N: tl.constexpr = 32
acc = tl.zeros((BLOCK_M, BLOCK_N), dtype=tl.float32)  # [2, 32]
for k_idx in range(0, tl.cdiv(K, BLOCK_K)):
    a = tl.load(A + ...)  # [2, 64]
    b = tl.load(B + ...)  # [64, 32]
    acc += tl.dot(a, b)
fast_pseudocode:
# BLOCK_N=64, BLOCK_K=64, BLOCK_M=2, block_size=32
# 16.9 KB dynamic smem/block, 126 regs/thread
# 17-way bank conflicts, 82.35% of wavefronts conflicting
BLOCK_N: tl.constexpr = 64
acc = tl.zeros((BLOCK_M, BLOCK_N), dtype=tl.float32)  # [2, 64]
for k_idx in range(0, tl.cdiv(K, BLOCK_K)):
    a = tl.load(A + ...)  # [2, 64]
    b = tl.load(B + ...)  # [64, 64]
    acc += tl.dot(a, b)
applicable_when: Never: this direction (doubling BLOCK_N when smem bank conflicts already dominate) consistently worsens performance by increasing smem footprint, bank conflict severity, and register pressure simultaneously.
do_not_apply_when: When NCU reports SharedMemoryConflicts with high bank conflict way (>=8x) and MIO stalls dominate CPI: doubling BLOCK_N increases the [BLOCK_K x BLOCK_N] shared memory tile, which amplifies rather than reduces bank conflicts. Also avoid when registers per thread are already high (>60) — a larger accumulator tile [BLOCK_M, BLOCK_N] will push register usage toward the hardware limit (255), reducing theoretical occupancy further.
framework_notes: In Triton, BLOCK_N is a tl.constexpr that controls the accumulator tile shape [BLOCK_M, BLOCK_N] and the B-tile shape [BLOCK_K, BLOCK_N] in shared memory. Doubling BLOCK_N doubles the B-tile footprint in shared memory, which increases bank conflict severity when the access stride is already misaligned. The register count scales with the accumulator tile size. The actual speedup of 1.3728x reported is the end-to-end benchmark speedup (likely from autotune selecting a better num_warps/num_stages config), not from the BLOCK_N change itself — the per-kernel profiling shows a 26% regression in duration (51.14 → 64.38 µs).
